query: Consider a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy coating on a Cu matrix under nanoindentation and friction conditions. The system is observed to have stable wear resistance and high elastic modulus at room temperature (300 K), but a sharp decline in wear resistance occurs at elevated temperatures. Given that lattice softening and atomic disorder are potential failure modes, how does the evolution of dislocation density and stacking fault structures with temperature explain the transition from stable to unstable wear behavior? Define the critical temperature threshold where the mechanism shifts from defect-mediated plasticity to rapid lattice disorder.

generation.hypothesis: In FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy coatings, the transition from stable to unstable wear behavior at elevated temperatures is driven by a shift from defect-mediated plasticity (dislocation glide and stacking fault formation) to rapid lattice disorder (lattice softening and enhanced atomic diffusion). Below a critical temperature threshold (~400-500 K), high stacking fault energy and sluggish diffusion stabilize dislocation structures, maintaining high elastic modulus and wear resistance. Above this threshold, thermal activation reduces stacking fault energy, promoting cross-slip and dislocation annihilation, while lattice softening accelerates atomic disorder, leading to catastrophic wear failure.
generation.material_initial_state: FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy coating on a Cu matrix, FCC single-phase structure with high dislocation density from deposition, stable at 300 K.
generation.intervention: Application of nanoindentation and friction under increasing temperature conditions (300 K to >500 K).
generation.conditions: Room temperature (300 K) to elevated temperatures (up to 600 K), atmospheric environment, sliding wear conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Evolution of dislocation density and stacking fault structures; transition from stable dislocation networks to lattice softening and atomic disorder.
generation.mechanism: At low temperatures, high stacking fault energy and sluggish diffusion stabilize dislocation glide and stacking faults, enabling work hardening and wear resistance. As temperature increases, stacking fault energy decreases, promoting cross-slip and dislocation annihilation. Concurrently, lattice softening and enhanced atomic diffusion lead to rapid loss of structural integrity, causing a sharp decline in wear resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Stable wear resistance and high elastic modulus at 300 K; sharp decline in wear resistance above ~450 K due to lattice softening and atomic disorder.
generation.baseline: Conventional HEAs show gradual degradation with temperature; FeNiCrCoCu exhibits a sharp transition due to unique stacking fault energy behavior.
generation.boundary: Valid for FeNiCrCoCu HEA coatings on Cu matrices under sliding wear; may not apply to refractory HEAs or different matrix materials.
generation.uncertainty: Exact critical temperature threshold may vary with coating microstructure, Cu matrix interaction, and specific alloy composition ratios. Limited direct experimental data on FeNiCrCoCu under combined nanoindentation and friction at elevated temperatures.
generation.falsification_experiment: Perform nanoindentation and pin-on-disk wear tests on FeNiCrCoCu coatings at incremental temperatures (300-600 K) while measuring dislocation density (via TEM) and stacking fault energy (via XRD line profile analysis). If wear resistance declines gradually rather than sharply above a specific temperature, or if dislocation density remains stable despite temperature increase, the hypothesis is falsified.

Microstructure of selective laser-melted equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy

Figure 1 shows an SEM-BSE image and EDS mapping results of as-built equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA. The BSE image revealed some micron-scale gas pores, but coarse defects or cracks were not observed in the as-built HEA (Porosity: 0.13%). The density of the present alloy was measured as 7.96 g/cm 3 which was similar to that of the theoretical density of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA. In addition, Co, Cr, Fe, Mn, and Ni were all around 20 at. % in EDS mapping analysis, and all elements were evenly distributed. Li et al . [38] found that Mn undergoes segregation when equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA is manufactured using SLM. According to Wang et al . [41] , when equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA was manufactured with pre-alloyed powder using electron beam melting (EBM), it was confirmed that Fe, Cr and Co elements segregate into the dendrite, whereas, Mn and Ni segregate into the interdendrite region. However, when the optimal process condition using SLM was deduced, no dendritic microstructure was formed, and it was possible to manufacture a random solid solution HEA with compositional homogeneity.

Abstract In this study, the wear behaviour of a powder metallurgically produced AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 high-entropy alloy (HEAs) is investigated at elevated temperatures. Spark plasma sintering (SPS) of inert gas atomised feedstock enables the production of dense bulk material. The microstructure evolution and phase formation are analysed. The high cooling rate in the atomisation process results in spherical powder with a microstructure comprising two finely distributed body-centred cubic phases. An additional phase with a complex crystal structure precipitates during SPS processing, while no coarsening of microstructural features occurs. The wear resistance under reciprocating wear conditions increases at elevated temperatures due to the formation of a protective oxide layer under atmospherical conditions. Additionally, the coefficient of friction (COF) slightly decreases with increasing temperature. SPS processing is suitable for the production of HEA bulk material. An increase in the wear resistance at elevated temperature enables high temperature applications of the HEA system AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 .
